title: Galatians
subtitle: Freedom in Christ, and who belongs to Abraham's family
lead: Galatians is Paul's most urgent letter. He wrote to churches he had founded, after other teachers arrived and told his Gentile converts that faith in Christ was not enough: they must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses to be full members of Abraham's family. Paul answers in anger and in earnest. He gives no thanks at the start, curses anyone who preaches a different good news, tells the story of his call and his meetings with the Jerusalem leaders, and describes his public clash with Cephas at Antioch. Then he argues from the Galatians' own experience of the Spirit, from Abraham, from the curse of the law and from baptism that all who belong to Christ are already Abraham's children and heirs of the promise: 'There is no Jew and no Greek... For all of you are one in Christ Jesus' (3:28).

The letter has shaped Christian teaching more than any other of its length. Luther's lectures on it made justification by faith the center of the Reformation; Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant readers still differ on 'works of the law', on 'the faith of Christ' and on the role of the law. It is also at the center of a modern argument over whether Paul left Judaism or lived and wrote within it, and of what 3:28 means for Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free, men and women. This site reads Galatians as a letter written by a Jew to Gentiles about how they belong to the people of the God of Israel, and gives the readings of the churches and of scholars side by side.
facts: Paul, undisputed by almost every scholar. He names 'all the brothers who are with me' as senders (1:2) and writes the closing lines himself, 'in large letters' (6:11).

Between about AD 48 and 57. On the South Galatian view (and with 2:1-10 as the famine visit), possibly the late 40s, before the Council of Acts 15; on the North Galatian view and with 2:1-10 as the Council, the mid-50s. See 'When was it written?' below.
Unknown. Antioch is proposed for an early date; Ephesus, Macedonia or Corinth for a later one.

A letter of rebuke and persuasion, built as an argument: opening (1:1-10), Paul's story (1:11-2:21), proofs from experience and Scripture (3:1-4:31), exhortation (5:1-6:10) and a closing in Paul's own hand (6:11-18).
Greek, with quotations from the Old Testament mostly in the Greek translation (the Septuagint).
authorship: Galatians is one of the seven letters that almost all scholars accept as Paul's own (with Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians and Philemon). Its style, its autobiography and its theme match Romans and the Corinthian letters. No case against it has persuaded scholars (a few nineteenth-century critics, the Dutch Radical school and Bruno Bauer, denied all of Paul's letters).
'All the brothers who are with me' (1:2) are not named. They may have been his fellow workers or the church in the place where he wrote. The Greek 'brothers' includes women.

At 6:11 Paul takes the pen from his scribe: 'See what large letters I make, writing with my own hand.' Ancient letter writers usually dictated, and added a closing greeting by hand. Whether the large letters meant poor eyesight (compare 4:15), emphasis, or the style of a notice is debated.

In about AD 140 Marcion, a teacher in Rome, put Galatians first in his collection of Paul's letters and read it as a proof that Paul had broken with the Old Testament. Tertullian and Epiphanius, who report this, argued against him; the church rejected his reading and his canon.

audience.to: Several churches in Galatia, founded by Paul: mostly Gentile believers who before their conversion had served gods that 'by nature are not gods' (4:8), with some Jewish believers among them. They had received the Spirit when they heard and believed the good news, with miracles (3:2-5). Whether these churches were in the northern region of Galatia around Ancyra, or in the southern cities of Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe (Acts 13-14), is disputed. They were small groups meeting in houses: in cities such as Pisidian Antioch and Iconium on the South Galatian view, in smaller towns and villages on the North Galatian view.
audience.why: After Paul left, other teachers came to the churches and told the Gentile believers that they needed circumcision and a Jewish way of life to belong to Abraham's family and be safe from the powers of the age. Paul heard of it and wrote. The question was not a matter of detail: if circumcision was needed, then faith in Christ was not enough, Christ's death was 'for no reason' (2:21), and the Gentiles' experience of the Spirit was not the whole truth. He needed to bring the Galatians back and to show them how Jews and Gentiles belong together in one family without one side taking on the other's identity.
views: Celtic Galatians of the old region around Ancyra, evangelized on the second and third journeys (Acts 16:6; 18:23); letter in the mid-50s.
The churches of Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe (Acts 13-14); letter possibly in the late 40s, before the Council.
The traditional view: teachers of the circumcision party, from Jerusalem or Judea.
The agitators were outsiders to the church
Mark Nanos: Jewish teachers in the synagogues who pressed Gentile Christians to complete conversion to be acceptable in the Jewish community.

lenses.name: History and setting
lenses.desc: Reads Galatians in its first-century setting: the Roman province and the old Celtic region of Galatia, the North and South Galatian theories, Paul's career between Damascus and Antioch, the meeting at Jerusalem and Acts 15, the clash at Antioch and the table, the agitators and the circumcision demand, and the Greek and Roman world of slaves, attendants, wills and the evil eye.

lenses.name: Critical
lenses.desc: Asks how the letter was made and how it is read: its rhetorical type (Betz's courtroom speech, Kennedy's deliberative speech), mirror-reading the opponents, the grammar of pistis Christou, the disputed 3:20, the elements of the world (stoicheia), the text (Papyrus 46, Papyrus 51, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Marcion) and the variants.

lenses.name: Literary
lenses.desc: Reads the letter's design: a rebuke in place of a thanksgiving, the story of Paul's life as argument, the proof from experience, from Abraham and from the curse, the allegory of Hagar and Sarah, the movement from narrative to argument to exhortation, and the recurring words 'good news', 'faith', 'promise', 'flesh' and 'Spirit'.

lenses.name: Jewish reading
lenses.desc: Reads Paul as a Jew writing to Gentiles: the New Perspective (Sanders, Dunn, Wright), the Paul-within-Judaism readings (Nanos, Gager, Eisenbaum, Fredriksen, Campbell, Boyarin), circumcision, covenant and Torah, 4QMMT and 'works of the law', God-fearers, Genesis 15 and 17, Habakkuk 2:4, Deuteronomy 21:23, Jewish readings of Hagar and Ishmael, and the table at Antioch.

lenses.name: Church tradition
lenses.desc: Follows how the churches have read Galatians: Origen, Chrysostom, Jerome and Augustine on the incident at Antioch, Luther's lectures of 1535, Calvin, Wesley, the Orthodox and Catholic readings, Trent session 6 and the 1999 Joint Declaration.

sections.b:
Galatians is a letter written in anger, and it is a letter of a particular kind: a rebuke that argues. Read it in one sitting, aloud, as the first churches heard it. It has four movements. First comes Paul's story (1:11-2:21), which proves his independence from Jerusalem and ends with his statement of the good news in 2:15-21. Second come the arguments (3:1-4:31) from the Galatians' own experience of the Spirit, from Scripture, from an everyday covenant, from the law's purpose, and from Hagar and Sarah. Third is the exhortation (5:1-6:10) to live in freedom and by the Spirit. Fourth is the closing in Paul's own hand (6:11-18).

Keep three questions in front of you. Who is Paul writing to, and what are they being told? What does he mean by 'works of the law' and 'justified'? And what is the law for? The notes and chapter pages give the main answers of the churches and of scholars.

sections.h: Who were the Galatians? North or South
sections.b: See the deep dive on chapter 1. In short: the Gauls settled in central Asia Minor in 278 BC; in 25 BC Augustus made Galatia a Roman province that also took in Pisidia and Lycaonia. The North Galatian view takes Paul to mean the old Celtic homeland; the South Galatian view takes him to mean the province, with its churches in Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe. Neither view settles the argument of the letter, but the choice affects the date and the way Galatians fits with Acts.

The date depends on two choices: where the Galatian churches were, and which visit to Jerusalem is the second visit of 2:1-10. (A) The South Galatian view with the famine visit of Acts 11:30 (Ramsay, Bruce, Longenecker): Galatians is written from Antioch about AD 48-49, before the Council of Acts 15, and is perhaps the earliest of Paul's letters; this explains why Paul does not cite the Council's letter. (B) The North Galatian view with the Council (Lightfoot, Betz): Galatians is written after the Council, in the mid-50s from Ephesus or Macedonia, close in time and thought to 2 Corinthians and Romans. The letter's themes and the language of 2:16, 3:6-14 and 4:1-7 are close to Romans (about AD 56-57), and that closeness to Romans is the common reason for the later dates, though similar themes could come from different times in Paul's work. These are not the only options: some scholars combine a South Galatian address with the Council of Acts 15, and others (Haenchen, Lüdemann) hold that Acts has told one Jerusalem visit twice. The Plain makes no choice.

Paul does not name the people who disturbed the churches. Mirror-reading uses his replies to rebuild what they said. The best-supported guesses are that they came after Paul left, taught that Gentile believers should be circumcised and keep the Jewish calendar (5:2-3; 4:10), appealed to the covenant with Abraham, and said that Paul's message came from Jerusalem and was inconsistent. John Barclay's 1987 article is the standard warning: mirror-reading can give a portrait of the opponents that is mostly Paul's own argument. See the deep dive on chapter 1.

PartPassageWhat Paul argues
Opening1:1-10Paul's authority is from Jesus Christ and God the Father; there is one good news, and a curse on any other.
Paul's story1:11-2:21He received the good news by revelation, was independent of Jerusalem, and was accepted by its leaders; he opposed Cephas when Cephas withdrew from the Gentiles' table; no one is justified by works of the law, but by faith in Christ.
Proofs3:1-4:31The Galatians received the Spirit by hearing with faith; Abraham was reckoned righteous by faith, and the promise to him cannot be canceled by the later law; the law was temporary, added on account of transgressions, an attendant until Christ; believers are sons and heirs; the Hagar and Sarah allegory.
Exhortation5:1-6:10Stand firm in freedom and do not accept circumcision; faith working through love; walk by the Spirit, not the flesh; the fruit of the Spirit; bear one another's burdens.
Closing6:11-18The agitators boast in the flesh; Paul boasts only in the cross; new creation is what counts; peace on 'the Israel of God'; the marks of Jesus on Paul's body.

Paul reads Scripture in Greek, mostly the Septuagint. His quotations sometimes differ from the Hebrew translated on this site. The notes give the Plain of the Old Testament verse wherever the book is already translated. The oldest witness is Papyrus 46 (about AD 200), a codex of Paul's letters that contains all of Galatians. Papyrus 51 (5th century) has parts of chapter 1. The great codices Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (300s), Alexandrinus and Ephraemi (400s), and the Western Claromontanus and Boernerianus have the whole letter. Marcion's text, reported by Tertullian and Epiphanius, put Galatians first. The Byzantine text adds a subscription saying the letter was written from Rome, which is clearly wrong, since nothing in it points to Rome. The variants that change the English are marked in the text: 1:3, 1:6, 1:10, 1:11, 1:15, 1:18, 2:4, 2:5, 2:9, 2:12, 2:16 (two entries), 2:20, 3:1, 3:12, 3:14, 3:17 and 3:22 are in the first part. The Plain follows the SBL text as its base. It departs from it at 1:3 (the NA28 reading 'God our Father') and at 1:15 (it includes 'God', as the NA28 and most editions do). At 2:16 and 3:22 the difference is in how the Greek 'faith of Jesus Christ' is read, not in the manuscripts. The variant entries give the KJV differences.

Origen wrote an early commentary (now lost, known through Jerome); Victorinus, Jerome (about AD 386-387) and Chrysostom followed, and Augustine wrote on it about AD 394-395. The debate between Jerome and Augustine on 2:11-14 shaped Western thinking about the truthfulness of Scripture. Martin Luther lectured on Galatians in 1516-17 (published 1519) and again in 1531 (published 1535), and is reported, in sayings recorded by others in his Table Talk, to have called it the letter he was 'betrothed' to, 'my Katie von Bora'; the lectures made justification by faith the center of the Lutheran Reformation. In May 1738, Charles Wesley read Luther's commentary on Galatians (17 May) and found peace (21 May). Three days later, at Aldersgate Street, John Wesley's heart was 'strangely warmed' while someone read aloud Luther's Preface to the Epistle to the Romans, not Galatians. Calvin's commentary (1548) and the Reformed reading stressed the three uses of the law. Catholic teaching responded with the Council of Trent (session 6, on justification); the 1999 Joint Declaration states the agreement now reached between Lutherans and Catholics.

Galatians has been used for centuries to say that Jews are slaves to a law that Christ ended, that Judaism is a religion of earning salvation, and that the church has replaced Israel. Christian anti-Judaism often appealed to the letter. Modern scholarship has questioned each of these. E. P. Sanders argued, and many scholars have come to accept, that first-century Judaism was a religion of grace and obedience in the covenant, not of earning (the picture is contested, notably by Stephen Westerholm); Krister Stendahl argued that Paul was called, not converted from Judaism; scholars of the 'Paul within Judaism' school (Nanos, Gager, Eisenbaum, Fredriksen) read the letter as Paul's argument for Gentiles, not against Jews. Jewish scholars such as Amy-Jill Levine and Marc Zvi Brettler, in the Jewish Annotated New Testament, ask Christian readers to hear the letter without the polemic, and Daniel Boyarin has argued that Paul's wish for a universal human unity has a cost for Jewish difference.

The letter itself contains hard words. Paul says that those under the law are under a curse (3:10), compares the Jerusalem of his day to Hagar and slavery (4:25), and says of the agitators, 'I wish they would cut themselves off' (5:12). Readers are asked to read these in their first setting: Paul, a Jew, writing in anger to Gentile Christians about a particular group of teachers. The Plain keeps the words as they are and gives the Jewish and Christian readings in the notes.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the letter was read aloud over a shared meal
spec.body: In the first century a letter to a church was read aloud when the assembly met, and in Paul's churches the assembly met for a meal. The issue Paul describes at Antioch was who may eat with whom (2:11-14). If Galatians was read at such a meal, the Gentile believers would have heard the story of Cephas withdrawing from the table while they sat at one, and the declaration 'there is no Jew and no Greek' (3:28) in the middle of their own shared supper. The letter's weight may then have been felt first as an event at a table. This overlaps with the observation, made by many scholars from Dunn to Nanos, that table fellowship was the chief place where the Jew-Gentile question was settled in practice, and with the ancient evidence that letters were read in assemblies. The new element is the suggestion that the letter's staging, and not only its argument, is part of its meaning.
spec.refs: Galatians 2:11-14; Galatians 3:26-29; Galatians 6:11; 1 Corinthians 11:17-34; Colossians 4:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:27

prompts:
An ancient room with a low table: Paul, a lean man with a weathered face (no description of his looks survives from his own time), leans forward over a long papyrus sheet and writes the last lines in big, rough Greek letters while a younger scribe stands aside with a reed pen in his hand; an oil lamp burns; scrolls lie in a basket; the sheet ends with the word 'Amen'.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment, with ancient manuscript borders, cave-painting ochre and soft modern watercolor washes; ink lines wobble a little, edges fade into rough parchment; no hard rectangular frame.

Two long low tables in a courtyard in Antioch, lamplit: at one table Gentile believers in plain Greek tunics, at the other Jewish believers in prayer shawls; a man in the middle with a rough fisherman's hands (Cephas) is half-risen from the Gentile table, looking at three newcomers standing in the doorway; another man, short and stern (Paul), stands at the head with a raised hand; a loaf and cups on both tables.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment, with ancient manuscript borders, cave-painting ochre and soft modern watercolor washes; edges fade into rough parchment; no hard rectangular frame.

Two women, back to back on an open plain, drawn like cave paintings: Hagar with a water skin and her young son Ishmael, walking out toward a wilderness; Sarah, holding Isaac, standing at the door of a tent; between them a faint line of mountains (Sinai on the left, a city on the right); stars above.

reading: Richard N. Longenecker, Galatians (Word Biblical Commentary 41, 1990)
A full commentary from a South Galatian, evangelical viewpoint, careful on the Greek and on Paul's chronology.
The classic rhetorical commentary, reading the letter as a speech for the defense.
James D. G. Dunn, The Epistle to the Galatians (Black's New Testament Commentaries, 1993)
The New Perspective's commentary, with much on works of the law and the Antioch incident.
An apocalyptic reading: the letter as a report of God's invasion of the world in Christ.
Thomas R. Schreiner, Galatians (Zondervan Exegetical Commentary, 2010) and Douglas J. Moo, Galatians (Baker Exegetical Commentary, 2013)
Two careful evangelical commentaries that keep the traditional reading and answer the New Perspective.
Martinus C. de Boer, Galatians (New Testament Library, 2011)
A recent critical commentary in the apocalyptic line.
Mark D. Nanos, The Irony of Galatians (2002)
A Paul-within-Judaism reading, with a new account of who the opponents were.
Richard B. Hays, The Faith of Jesus Christ (2nd ed., 2002)
The study that opened the modern debate over 'the faith of Christ', with Dunn's reply.
Martin Luther, Lectures on Galatians (1535), Luther's Works vols. 26-27
The classic Protestant reading, long and direct.

traditions.q: How have the churches read Galatians as a whole?
views: Galatians is the charter of justification by faith alone. Luther lectured on it in 1531 and published the lectures in 1535; in sayings recorded by others in his Table Talk he is reported to have called it the letter he was 'betrothed' to, 'my Katie von Bora'. In it the law shows sin and drives to Christ, and the believer receives Christ's righteousness as a gift.
Calvin's commentary (1548) reads the letter as a defense of free justification against the merit of works, and Reformed teaching on the three uses of the law draws on 3:19-24 and 5:13-26.

The Church reads Galatians within the whole of Scripture and tradition: Aquinas' commentary stresses grace and the Spirit, and the Council of Trent (session 6) denies that works done without grace justify while affirming that faith works through love (5:6). In 1999 Catholics and Lutherans issued a Joint Declaration on justification.

The Orthodox read Galatians through Chrysostom's commentary and stress freedom in Christ and life in the Spirit; 'Christ lives in me' (2:20) is read as union with Christ (theosis), not mainly as a court verdict.

Wesley's Notes read Galatians as a call to faith that works by love and to holiness by the Spirit; in May 1738 Charles Wesley read Luther on Galatians before he found peace, and three days later John Wesley's heart was 'strangely warmed' at Aldersgate Street as Luther's Preface to Romans was read (not Galatians).

Article 11 on justification and the Homily on Salvation rest on Galatians and Romans; Anglicans include Evangelicals who stress justification by faith and Anglo-Catholics who stress the sacraments and sanctification.
Pentecostal teaching points to 3:2-5 and 3:14, which make the gift of the Spirit the proof of the good news, and to 5:16-26 on life in the Spirit.
